How Beta Technologies Is Clearing the Runway for Electric Flight

📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 27 min read (5436 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~27 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It aims to lift the industry with its aircraft, motors, batteries, and charging network.
  • Beta Technologies, one of the top three U.S.
  • In the cockpit of Beta Technologies’ Alia CX300, pilot Chris Caputo steers onto Runway 33 at Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport in Vermont.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It aims to lift the industry with its aircraft, motors, batteries, and charging network.

Beta Technologies, one of the top three U.S. electric aircraft makers, is aiming first at regional cargo and medical transport, before pursuing the passenger market. Shown here is Beta’s Alia A250, for vertical takeoffs and landings.

In the cockpit of Beta Technologies’ Alia CX300, pilot Chris Caputo steers onto Runway 33 at Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport in Vermont. Cleared for takeoff, he releases the brakes and nudges the throttle forward.

At the back of the aircraft, the five-blade pusher propeller snaps awake, and the Alia bolts forward. There’s no shriek of a turbofan spooling up, no shudder of a piston engine, and no wait for thrust. Just the low hum of an electric motor and a shove of instant acceleration.

Within a few seconds, we’re at 85 knots (almost 160 kilometers per hour), and Caputo rotates the nose upward. The runway drops abruptly away as we climb. Gaining speed and altitude, we head northwest over Lake Champlain. Through the wraparound canopy, I watch the hunched shoulders of Vermont’s Green Mountains shrink under the right wing, with New York’s taller Adirondacks to the left.

According to recent reports, caputo, a former Air Force fighter pilot, flicks the control stick hard left, then right. Despite its 15-meter wingspan, the Alia feels snappy, its fly-by-wire system automatically coordinating aileron and rudder inputs. The machine, he indicates, is much simpler to manage than the Cessna 182 I flew around Australia in my student-pilot days.

What’s more, our half-hour flight in the Alia will consume only about US $9 worth of electricity. The same flight in a comparable Cessna 208 Caravan would burn roughly 25 to 30 gallons of Jet A fuel, costing about $210 to $255 at press time. “Even at full throttle, we’re not burning any fuel up here,” states Caputo, as he takes the Alia into a sweeping left turn and heads south over the lake. “We’re not polluting the environment. [There’s] no noise pollution.”.

In a recent development, at Beta’s South Burlington, Vt., facility, workers assemble the body of an Alia A250. The company states it has an order and option-to-buy backlog of nearly 1,000 aircraft.Beta Technologies.

This ride is happening during an unusually lively time for electric aviation. The promise of lower operating costs and cleaner flight has pushed electric aircraft from a fringe experiment to one of the aviation industry’s most closely watched frontiers. After years of renderings, prototypes, and overly optimistic timetables, companies are now flying full-size aircraft, submitting hardware to regulators for certification, building factories, and testing routes with prospective customers.

Among the top three U.S. developers of electric planes, Archer Aviation and Joby Aviation are concentrating on piloted vertical-takeoff-and-landing air taxis, otherwise known as eVTOLs. Beta Technologies is taking a broader—and in some ways more innovative—path into the market. Rather than betting first on air taxis, Beta is looking to enter electric aviation through short-haul freight planes that use conventional runways, fed by an open charging network that’s designed to make electric aircraft—both Beta’s and its competitors’—part of a working transportation system.

According to recent reports, to that end, the manufacturer is developing two variants of its Alia airframe: the runway-based CX300 I’m flying in and the A250, which adds four lift propellers for vertical takeoff and landing. Beta indicates its test pilots have flown the Alia family more than 300,000 kilometers, including doing multiple U.S. crossings and overseas demonstrations. The company claims an order and option-to-buy backlog of 991 aircraft.

RELATED: From Hockey Enforcer to High-Flying eVTOL CEO.

“We’re taking a pragmatic stepwise approach for both certification and market entry,” notes Beta’s CEO and founder Kyle Clark. “We’re ready to go today with medical and cargo aircraft that fly from airport to airport.” Next up, he says, will be passenger aircraft with conventional takeoff and landing, followed by cargo eVTOLs, and finally passenger eVTOLs.

Beta’s 17,500-square-meter production facility sits beside the Burlington airport and looks more like a giant sunlit workshop than a conventional airplane factory. Geothermal heat pumps help heat and cool the structure. The roof will eventually hold a megawatt of solar panels. On the floor, technicians make composite structures and join aircraft sections beneath American and Pride flags.

3 Competing Paths to Electric AviationThe top three U.S. electric-aircraft makers are taking different approaches to the same challenge: how to make short-hop flight cleaner, quieter, and commercially useful.aspect_ratioJoby Aviation’s piloted, four-passenger S4 aircraft has six tilting propellers to provide both vertical lift and cruise propulsion. It’s optimized for fast, quiet air-taxi service. The manufacturer is also working on hydrogen fuel cells for longer-range transport. Joby says the S4 is in the final stage of the Federal Aviation Administration’s certification process and has flown trials in Dubai, New York, and Texas.Archer Aviation’s piloted, four-passenger Midnight has 12 propellers—six tilting rotors and six stationary rotors. The aircraft, which Archer has been testing in both vertical and conventional takeoffs and landings, is aimed at air-taxi service in urban areas. The company says Midnight is in Phase 4 of the FAA certification process and has completed trial flights.Beta Technologies’ piloted Alia aircraft comes in two flavors: The A250 eVTOL has separate vertical-lift rotors and a rear cruise propeller, while the CX300 is a conventional-takeoff fixed-wing plane. The two models use the same pusher motor, battery pack, flight control computer, and fixed-pitch propeller. The company is initially focusing on cargo and medical transport, regional logistics, and airport-to-airport operations, with passenger service later. Beta expects FAA certification for the CX300 in 2027 and for the A250 a year later.Kyle Clark, a native of Vermont, founded Beta in 2017 to realize his long-held dream of building a hybrid-electric aircraft. (For his bachelor’s thesis at Harvard University, he designed a flight-control system for such an aircraft.) Martine Rothblatt, CEO of the biotech company United Therapeutics and cofounder of SiriusXM satellite radio, invested $48 million in Beta to fund its first prototype, with the eventual goal of using the aircraft to transport organs for transplantation.The company has kept much of its design and manufacturing in-house, partly because the pieces are closely coupled and partly because suitable aviation components didn’t exist when development began. Vertical integration gives Beta’s engineers control over the interfaces and any failure data. But it also means the company must be competent at several businesses simultaneously: airframes, electric motors, inverters, batteries, software, chargers, and aircraft production.The production line can build both the fixed-wing CX300 and the vertical-lift A250, which share the same fuselage, wings, pusher motor (for horizontal propulsion), batteries, avionics, and much of the tooling. This results in some one-size-fits-all decisions: The CX300’s twin booms, which connect the wing to the tail surfaces, look superfluous until you see the A250’s four lift propellers mounted on similar structures.On the CX300, those booms add weight and drag even though they serve no lift function. But the trade-off—a simpler overall design—is part of Beta’s central strategy: Rather than applying for FAA certification for the more novel and complex eVTOL A250, with its multiple lift systems and transitions between hover and wing-borne flight, the company is bringing the runway version forward first. It’s certifying the motor, batteries, fly-by-wire controls, and much of the airframe in the simpler aircraft; it will then reuse evidence and manufacturing experience when it certifies the A250.The other substantial reason to start with the CX300 is logistical: The United States has more than 5,000 public-use airports, so the CX300 can operate from infrastructure that already exists. The cargo and medical flights that the aircraft will initially tackle offer tightly defined missions in which lower energy and maintenance costs matter more than cabin amenities. Hence the company’s decision to leave cabin air-conditioning off the CX300, at least for now. “Things that don’t exist on an airplane don’t weigh anything,” Clark says. “They can’t break. You don’t have to service them…. You don’t have to certify them.”“This strategy, at the beginning, was seen as a failure of their VTOL,” says analyst Sergio Cecutta, a managing partner at SMG Consulting. “But I think a lot of people were very myopic. It was a way for [Beta] to break up the certification in two pieces, and so they have retired a lot of the risk. [A majority] of the [CX300’s] parts are shared with the VTOL, and that means that a lot of the documentation for certification can be easily reused on the VTOL side when that certification starts.”How Redundancy Enhances SafetyA decade and a half after electric cars began making significant inroads into the automotive market, electric airplane technology is advancing rapidly. In some ways, an electric car has more complicated power-engineering requirements than an electric aircraft. An electric car’s power demands change constantly, while an electric aircraft operates in a narrower set of power regimes: takeoff, level flight, and descent.But if your car’s drivetrain fails, you can just pull over to the side of the road. That’s not an option for a pilot 1,000 meters up. The hurdle isn’t that electric motors are inherently fragile; it’s that aviation safety standards are extraordinarily demanding. Catastrophic failure conditions generally must be held to roughly one chance in a billion flight hours or less.The two versions of Beta’s Alia aircraft—the A250 [shown] and the CX300—share many of the same components, which the company believes will speed up FAA certification.Beta TechnologiesBecause individual electrical components cannot meet that standard on their own, electric aircraft rely on layered redundancy: duplicate power paths, independent inverters, fault isolation, monitoring, and backup capacity. Each layer helps close the safety gap, but each also adds weight and complexity.To close the reliability gap and satisfy regulators who have little experience with electric aircraft, Beta engineers have built redundancy into the motor itself. When I visit the company’s motor shop, technicians are assembling the H500A pusher motor, which splits up critical components like the inverters and stator sections.“You could lose an entire half of the system, and it would still function the same,” says Adam Lowe, Beta’s flight operations lead.The H500A’s broad diameter gives the magnetic forces greater leverage, producing high torque at low rotational speed, a useful trait when turning large propellers. The H500A weighs about 75 kilograms and produces about 640 kilowatts of power. The motor achieves 97.5 percent efficiency, based on internal testing; typical conventional turboprops have an efficiency range of 25 to 35 percent.Beta had aimed to have its motor certified in the first half of 2026, a deadline that passed without a public announcement. Although the company’s certification strategy is aimed at streamlining the process, getting clearance to fly from the Federal Aviation Administration is probably still its biggest obstacle. For Beta, and any company trying to bring an electric aircraft into service, the FAA must sign off first on the propeller, then the motor, then the aircraft. After that, the manufacturer must pursue a production certificate from the FAA, proving that the company can build the same approved aircraft again and again, with the right tools, records, inspections, quality controls, supplier oversight, training, calibration, and parts tracking.Beta has found a narrow on-ramp to get the A250 flying before full certification. Under the FAA’s eVTOL Integration Pilot Program, companies and public agencies can run FAA-supervised, real-world trials to test how advanced air-mobility aircraft might operate in the national airspace. For Beta, that included July flights of the CX300 across a Virginia-to-Maryland corridor carrying, among other things, a manufactured transplantable organ in a medical containment system. Beta has also been chosen for six other FAA-backed trials.For the fixed-wing Alia CX300, customer trials are moving in parallel. In March, Beta’s CX300 successfully completed 23 flights over 10 days on Loganair routes linking six Scottish cities. The airline has since signed a term sheet for five Beta aircraft, with options for five more and service expected to start in 2029.Innovation in eVTOLsBeta is pushing so hard for the A250 because the case for electric flight gets even more interesting with vertical-lift aircraft. Helicopters and other VTOLs have a less orderly life than fixed-wing planes do. They must hover, sidestep, turn in place, settle, climb, and hold themselves in the air by main force. But conventional helicopters are built around a rotor speed that varies only a few percent because the engine, transmission, and rotor system are all designed around one narrow operating point.“One of the dreams of vertical flight has been to vary the rotor rpm,” says Anubhav Datta, an aerospace engineering professor at the University of Maryland, College Park, who studies electric propulsion and vertical flight. Electric motors, he argues, have advanced enough to make that practical. A rotor that can slow down or speed up as conditions change can waste less energy, make less noise, and better match the odd assortment of tasks that vertical flight demands.Electric propulsion also lets designers break up the work with multiple motors. The weight of an electric motor is tied closely to its torque. If you spread that torque among several motors, each of the motors can shrink, meaning that their combined weight is less than would be needed for one big engine. This is one reason why so many electric aircraft designs appear to have sprouted propellers wherever an engineer found a place to put one.There is a downside to using multiple smaller motors: If one of the motors quits, the rotor it’s driving has little stored energy compared to the inertia in a conventional helicopter’s one large rotor. This inertia can come in handy if the engine dies, because the rotor will continue to spin and allow the pilot to descend under control, in an emergency technique known as autorotation. Beta Technologies, Made in Vermont Beta TechnologiesAccording to Beta Technologies founder and CEO Kyle Clark, his native Vermont—known more for its maple syrup and outdoorsy lifestyle than its technological achievements—is a big part of the secret to Beta’s success at attracting talent. “The recruiting strategy is this: You find anybody who has vacationed in Vermont or went to school here. And you say, ‘You can actually live here and have a high-paying job in a mission-driven business, doing something that you care about with great people.’ ” The company presently employs about 1,500 people, most of them in South Burlington, Vt., and is actively hiring for its engineering, manufacturing, software, flight operations, and commercial teams.As befits an aviation company, Beta offers flying lessons for all employees—a perk that is intended to give engineers, software developers, pilots, and mechanics a common language. The company also operates a health clinic for employees and their families and is building a day care center. Those programs have an idealistic Vermont flavor that is shaped by Clark and his wife, Katie Clark, who is Beta’s head of brand, creative, culture and spaces. But they also serve a practical purpose: attracting and retaining the best people in a small labor market. —T.C.

3 Competing Paths to Electric Aviation.

Industry observers note that kyle Clark, a native of Vermont, founded Beta in 2017 to realize his long-held dream of building a hybrid-electric aircraft. (For his bachelor’s thesis at Harvard University, he designed a flight-control system for such an aircraft.) Martine Rothblatt, CEO of the biotech company United Therapeutics and cofounder of SiriusXM satellite radio, invested $48 million in Beta to fund its first prototype, with the eventual goal of using the aircraft to transport organs for transplantation.

The company has kept much of its design and manufacturing in-house, partly because the pieces are closely coupled and partly because suitable aviation components didn’t exist when development began. Vertical integration gives Beta’s engineers control over the interfaces and any failure data. But it also means the company must be competent at several businesses simultaneously: airframes, electric motors, inverters, batteries, software, chargers, and aircraft production.

Industry observers note that the production line can build both the fixed-wing CX300 and the vertical-lift A250, which share the same fuselage, wings, pusher motor (for horizontal propulsion), batteries, avionics, and much of the tooling. This results in some one-size-fits-all decisions: The CX300’s twin booms, which connect the wing to the tail surfaces, look superfluous until you see the A250’s four lift propellers mounted on similar structures.

On the CX300, those booms add weight and drag even though they serve no lift function. But the trade-off—a simpler overall design—is part of Beta’s central strategy: Rather than applying for FAA certification for the more novel and complex eVTOL A250, with its multiple lift systems and transitions between hover and wing-borne flight, the company is bringing the runway version forward first. It’s certifying the motor, batteries, fly-by-wire controls, and much of the airframe in the simpler aircraft; it will then reuse evidence and manufacturing experience when it certifies the A250.

It has been revealed that the other big reason to start with the CX300 is logistical: The United States has more than 5,000 public-use airports, so the CX300 can operate from infrastructure that already exists. The cargo and medical flights that the aircraft will initially tackle offer tightly defined missions in which lower energy and maintenance costs matter more than cabin amenities. Hence the company’s decision to leave cabin air-conditioning off the CX300, at least for now. “Things that don’t exist on an airplane don’t weigh anything,” Clark claims. “They can’t break. You don’t have to service them…. You don’t have to certify them.”.

In a recent development, “This strategy, at the beginning, was seen as a failure of their VTOL,” notes analyst Sergio Cecutta, a managing partner at SMG Consulting. “But I think a lot of people were very myopic. It was a way for [Beta] to break up the certification in two pieces, and so they have retired a lot of the risk. [A majority] of the [CX300’s] parts are shared with the VTOL, and that means that a lot of the documentation for certification can be easily reused on the VTOL side when that certification starts.”.

It has been revealed that A decade and a half after electric cars began making significant inroads into the automotive market, electric airplane technology is advancing rapidly. In some ways, an electric car has more complicated power-engineering requirements than an electric aircraft. An electric car’s power demands change constantly, while an electric aircraft operates in a narrower set of power regimes: takeoff, level flight, and descent.

It has been revealed that but if your car’s drivetrain fails, you can just pull over to the side of the road. That’s not an option for a pilot 1,000 meters up. The hurdle isn’t that electric motors are inherently fragile; it’s that aviation safety standards are extraordinarily demanding. Catastrophic failure conditions generally must be held to roughly one chance in a billion flight hours or less.

The two versions of Beta’s Alia aircraft—the A250 [shown] and the CX300—share many of the same components, which the tech giant believes will speed up FAA certification.

Because individual electrical components cannot meet that standard on their own, electric aircraft rely on layered redundancy: duplicate power paths, independent inverters, fault isolation, monitoring, and backup capacity. Each layer helps close the safety gap, but each also adds weight and complexity.

Recent findings suggest that to close the reliability gap and satisfy regulators who have little experience with electric aircraft, Beta engineers have built redundancy into the motor itself. When I visit the firm’s motor shop, technicians are assembling the H500A pusher motor, which splits up critical components like the inverters and stator sections.

“You could lose an entire half of the system, and it would still function the same,” claims Adam Lowe, Beta’s flight operations lead.

The H500A’s broad diameter gives the magnetic forces greater leverage, producing high torque at low rotational speed, a useful trait when turning large propellers. The H500A weighs about 75 kilograms and produces about 640 kilowatts of power. The motor achieves 97.5 percent efficiency, based on internal testing; typical conventional turboprops have an efficiency range of 25 to 35 percent.

Recent findings suggest that beta had aimed to have its motor certified in the first half of 2026, a deadline that passed without a public announcement. Although the tech giant’s certification strategy is aimed at streamlining the process, getting clearance to fly from the Federal Aviation Administration is probably still its biggest obstacle. For Beta, and any company trying to bring an electric aircraft into service, the FAA must sign off first on the propeller, then the motor, then the aircraft. After that, the manufacturer must pursue a production certificate from the FAA, proving that the company can build the same approved aircraft again and again, with the right tools, records, inspections, quality controls, supplier oversight, training, calibration, and parts tracking.

Beta has found a narrow on-ramp to get the A250 flying before full certification. Under the FAA’s eVTOL Integration Pilot Program, companies and public agencies can run FAA-supervised, real-world trials to test how advanced air-mobility aircraft might operate in the national airspace. For Beta, that included July flights of the CX300 across a Virginia-to-Maryland corridor carrying, among other things, a manufactured transplantable organ in a medical containment system. Beta has also been chosen for six other FAA-backed trials.

Sources indicate that for the fixed-wing Alia CX300, customer trials are moving in parallel. In March, Beta’s CX300 successfully completed 23 flights over 10 days on Loganair routes linking six Scottish cities. The airline has since signed a term sheet for five Beta aircraft, with options for five more and service expected to start in 2029.

Beta is pushing so hard for the A250 because the case for electric flight gets even more interesting with vertical-lift aircraft. Helicopters and other VTOLs have a less orderly life than fixed-wing planes do. They must hover, sidestep, turn in place, settle, climb, and hold themselves in the air by main force. But conventional helicopters are built around a rotor speed that varies only a few percent because the engine, transmission, and rotor system are all designed around one narrow operating point.

Recent findings suggest that “One of the dreams of vertical flight has been to vary the rotor rpm,” says Anubhav Datta, an aerospace engineering professor at the University of Maryland, College Park, who studies electric propulsion and vertical flight. Electric motors, he argues, have advanced enough to make that practical. A rotor that can slow down or speed up as conditions change can waste less energy, make less noise, and better match the odd assortment of tasks that vertical flight demands.

According to recent reports, electric propulsion also lets designers break up the work with multiple motors. The weight of an electric motor is tied closely to its torque. If you spread that torque among several motors, each of the motors can shrink, meaning that their combined weight is less than would be needed for one big engine. This is one reason why so many electric aircraft designs appear to have sprouted propellers wherever an engineer found a place to put one.

There is a downside to using multiple smaller motors: If one of the motors quits, the rotor it’s driving has little stored energy compared to the inertia in a conventional helicopter’s one large rotor. This inertia can come in handy if the engine dies, because the rotor will continue to spin and allow the pilot to descend under control, in an emergency technique known as autorotation.

Recent findings suggest that according to Beta Technologies founder and CEO Kyle Clark, his native Vermont—known more for its maple syrup and outdoorsy lifestyle than its technological achievements—is a significant part of the secret to Beta’s success at attracting talent. “The recruiting strategy is this: You find anybody who has vacationed in Vermont or went to school here. And you say, ‘You can actually live here and have a high-paying job in a mission-driven business, doing something that you care about with great people.’ ” The organization right now employs about 1,500 people, most of them in South Burlington, Vt., and is actively hiring for its engineering, manufacturing, software, flight operations, and commercial teams.

As befits an aviation company, Beta offers flying lessons for all employees—a perk that is intended to give engineers, software developers, pilots, and mechanics a common language. The company also operates a health clinic for employees and their families and is building a day care center. Those programs have an idealistic Vermont flavor that is shaped by Clark and his wife, Katie Clark, who is Beta’s head of brand, creative, culture and spaces. But they also serve a practical purpose: attracting and retaining the best people in a small labor market. —T.C.

In a recent development, electric-aircraft makers compensate with redundant motors and electrical channels, but most leading designs also have wings to allow gliding. In Beta’s A250, that means that if all else fails, the pilot still has a shot at reaching a suitable landing spot.

Sources indicate that that helps explain the convergence in today’s eVTOL designs. Joby Aviation’s S4 uses six propellers that tilt between lift and cruise. Archer Aviation’s Midnight has six tilting propellers and six dedicated lift props. Beta’s A250 keeps its four lift propellers horizontal and uses a separate pusher motor for forward flight.

It has been revealed that in Beta’s home state of Vermont, the electricity produced in the state comes almost entirely from renewable sources. Of course, electric aviation’s climate advantage depends not only on how clean the power grid is, but on how efficiently the aircraft uses energy. The turbines in conventional jet engines are marvelous machines, but they throw away a lot of energy as heat. Plus they need to carry the hardware to manage that heat—inlets, ducts, radiators, oil coolers—and the drag that comes with pulling air through all of it.

Kyle Clark [in cockpit], founder and CEO of Beta Technologies, pilots the firm’s Alia CX300, an electric plane that Beta expects to receive FAA certification in 2027. Clark began designing a hybrid electric plane while still in college.Beta Technologies.

By contrast, an electric design, with no combustion, gearbox, or oil circuits, avoids much of that energy burden. The result is an aircraft that is more than twice as “slippery” in terms of its lift-to-drag ratio. Batteries will never come close to the fuel density of petroleum fuels. But because electric drivetrains are much more efficient than combustion engines, a battery doesn’t necessarily need to match the energy density of petroleum fuel to be useful.

While the motors on an electric aircraft provide the drama at takeoff and landing, the batteries set nearly every boundary: the range, payload, charge time, cooling load, reserve energy, and, ultimately, useful life. For now, the hardest limit on electric aviation is not imagination, software, or even motors. It is the stubborn weight of stored energy.

Recent findings suggest that “One thing you notice about [electric] airplanes is that they are all small,” states Cecutta, the aviation analyst. “They are not small because someone has done a market study and decided that is the optimal size. They are small because you cannot make them major. This limitation is from the batteries.”.

Recent findings suggest that in a conventional aircraft, fuel accounts for a significant percentage of the takeoff weight. But that weight gradually disappears during flight. In an electric plane, the battery packs also account for a lot of the weight; in Beta’s CX300, they’re close to half the aircraft’s mass. But a drained battery at landing weighs the same as a fully charged one at takeoff. That means the rest of the aircraft must be light enough to lift a power source that never gets lighter, yet strong enough to endure vibration, turbulence, hard landings, and years of fatigue. The more engineers push to save weight, Datta notes, the more flexible the airframe becomes, making the wings and other structures more prone to bending, twisting, and vibration. In that sense, the battery problem becomes a structural problem, too.

Recent findings suggest that beta’s CX300 carries five liquid-cooled battery packs of about 45 kilowatt-hours each, giving the aircraft roughly 225 kWh of rated capacity, though not all of that may be usable in flight. Each pack weighs 255 kg and contains 2,772 cylindrical cells. Altogether, about 14,000 cells sit beneath the occupied cabin, each one a tiny storehouse of energy, heat, and potential trouble.

The burden of the battery explains much of what I see elsewhere in Beta’s aircraft: the 15-meter wingspan, the composite structure, and the almost doctrinal effort to leave out every piece of hardware and creature comfort that’s not essential to the mission. The CX300 even does without flaps, which most aircraft use to generate extra lift at low speeds, so it must take off and land unusually fast for an aircraft of its size.

It has been revealed that on Beta’s battery line, commercially supplied standard 21-millimeter-diameter, 70-mm-long cells are tested and assembled. Cells become modules, modules become subpacks, and eleven subpacks become a 45-kWh pack. Cooling plates manage heat during normal operation, while passive barriers and electrical isolation are designed to contain the ugly edge cases that Beta’s testing process intentionally triggers.

The modular design of the packs will give Beta’s planes a path to better batteries as the cells and battery chemistry improve. Caputo tells me that the firm is already evaluating higher-density cells at its battery testing facility in nearby St. Albans, Vt. More watt-hours per kilogram could eventually mean more range, more payload, or both.

What sets Beta Technologies apart from its competitors is the breadth of its ambitions: It’s not just building electric aircraft. It’s also cultivating a broader ecosystem to nurture the growth of electric aviation.

Sources indicate that for instance, Beta intends its motor business to extend beyond its own aircraft. The tech giant has delivered lift motors for Eve Air Mobility’s proof-of-concept aircraft and has a contract to supply up to $1 billion in pusher motors as Eve’s program develops. In addition, Beta is selling flight-control computers and software to Horizon Aircraft. It is also producing propulsion systems for the military, as well as the MV250, a hybrid-electric autonomous aircraft for defense missions.

Industry observers note that beta’s fast-charging stations [left] have been installed at 138 locations. The thermal-management station [right] keeps the battery from overheating during charging. The organization uses the open-standard Combined Charging System (CCS) so that other aircraft can use its chargers. Beta Technologies.

Sources indicate that further evidence of Beta’s far-ranging plans is visible near the battery line in the South Burlington facility, where workers are readying a few of the organization’s 1.5-meter-tall Charge Cubes for shipping. Intended for installation at airports, each cube takes 480-volt AC from the grid and can deliver up to 320 kW at as much as 1,000 volts DC. According to Beta, charging either model of its Alia aircraft takes about 35 minutes, from the minimum charge required under visual flight rules to full state. A separate thermal-management cube circulates water-glycol coolant through the aircraft to keep the batteries from overheating during charging.

Industry observers note that the charge cubes use the Combined Charging System (CCS), an open standard increasingly shared across the electric transportation industry. Beta’s strategy resembles Tesla’s decision to treat charging as part of the vehicle business, with one crucial difference: Beta is courting other aircraft makers, airports, and operators to use its technology. Archer, Atlantic Aviation, Signature Aviation, and government agencies have purchased or installed Beta’s charging equipment. As of October, Beta has 138 fast-charge locations, with additional sites in permitting or construction.

Sources indicate that for charging beyond the fixed network, Beta offers a wheeled 40-kW Mini Cube and a 65-kW Mini Cube+ that can ride inside an Alia and plug into more modest electrical service. The Mini Cube can also charge cars, buses, and trucks—any vehicle that uses the CCS standard.

Back above Lake Champlain, the CX300 levels off, and the motor recedes to a faint hum. Then Caputo switches it off, and there’s nothing but the rush of wind around the canopy. The aircraft glides on its long wings while the coasting propeller turns the motor into a generator, feeding about 9 kW back to the battery.

According to recent reports, then we turn to the east and slip into the landing queue behind a National Guard C-130 Hercules, and Caputo powers and slides the throttle forward. The motor springs to life again, pushing the airplane, and perhaps aviation itself, into the future.

#74163. My monitor was cutting my download speed by 75%

My monitor was cutting my download speed by 75%

📅 2026-11-15 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1536 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tymscar

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, somehow I am one of those few very lucky people to have the opportunity of owning a 2.5 gig symmetrical line for my internet.
  • It’s run by this one guy (Hey Keith!), and I know I can always message them and they respond promptly, as they did this time.
  • I didn’t have time for debugging, because I needed to travel 2000 km to the other side of the continent for a family emergency.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, somehow I am one of those few very lucky people to have the opportunity of owning a 2.5 gig symmetrical line for my internet. But one day, when I wanted to brag to my equally nerdy friends, shock and horror: 600 Mbps down? Luckily my upload speed was still 2.4 Gbps, so I didn’t lose all my bragging rights, but that’s weird, right? If anything, you’d expect the opposite!

My ISP is pretty cool. It’s run by this one guy (Hey Keith!), and I know I can always message them and they respond promptly, as they did this time. We tried to run through a few debugging steps, they checked on their end, and everything was normal. I tried my work laptop too, same speed.

I didn’t have time for debugging, because I needed to travel 2000 km to the other side of the continent for a family emergency.

In a recent development, but as soon as I got back, I got curious again. What could it be? In retrospect, I now know when it started: when I moved all my connections onto my Studio Display XDR. I wanted to have a one-cable setup, and the monitor offered me that. I’ve had it for half a year now, and I don’t think I’ve ever run a speed test through it. 600 Mbps was more than fast enough for me to never realise I wasn’t getting three quarters of the speed I was paying for 🤦.

Pings to other wired computers during a download would fail 10% of the time over Ethernet through the adapter plugged into my screen, and 0% of the time over Wi-Fi. What made it stranger was that there were no dropped frame errors in macOS’s logs at all. This was the substantial hint for me: the adapter was dropping them before the computer could know.

Industry observers note that I then plugged the adapter straight into my Mac instead of the monitor, and ran an iperf3 server on my UDR 7: 2.3 Gbps. So the cable, the router and the adapter are all fine? What about fast.com? Perfect speeds there too! 2.2 down and 2.3 up when connected straight in. As soon as I connected it to the display, it was back to 600 down again.

So it’s the display, right? Well, I would find out: sort of yes, sort of no, which is why I wanted to write this blog post. I couldn’t find anything online explaining the exact cause, and it’s quite a cool reason.

According to recent reports, the adapter uses a Realtek RTL8156B, which on macOS binds to Apple’s generic USB networking driver. But Realtek ship their own driver on their website, so I thought I’d give that a go! I installed it and, to my surprise, it almost doubled the download speed to 1.1 Gbps, but that was still nowhere close to 2.5. First hint that it couldn’t just be the monitor’s fault.

Then I tried flow control. I had never truly looked into this before, and I think it’s quite neat to know about if you were also ignorant of it like me. Basically, when a device receives Ethernet frames it can’t keep up with, it just drops them. With flow control (it’s something your router or switch has to support), it can send the sender a “pause” frame, and the sender then buffers the data on its side, instead of the receiver (the adapter in this case) on its side. I turned it on in my UniFi console and guess what, download jumped to around 2 Gbps, with upload still at full speed! Yay! Well, not so fast….

According to recent reports, I don’t like it always being on, because it can add latency to other systems like my gaming PC. Can you work around it? For sure, you can disable it on those computers, but it’s janky, and it’s another thing I need to remember when my Sauerbraten game starts lagging. I need fewer things to remember, considering I am 30 in a couple of months. My memory is not what it used to be.

Yeah, isn’t that weird? First of all, it looks like the port can indeed do 2.5 in both directions. I already knew that, because I get much more than that from my external SSD through the monitor’s Thunderbolt port. So the concern is not the monitor again? But it has to be!

According to recent reports, well, I had another idea. How about I connect to my Linux box, which is also on 2.5, and send perfectly smooth UDP traffic at a fixed rate with flow control off? Then I can check the chip’s own counter of dropped frames:.

Industry observers note that so basically no drops whatsoever when connected straight to my Mac, but loads of drops after about 168k frames per second (roughly 2 Gbps). Remember that number. That number comes from the adapter’s own counters: however much I sent, the number of frames it managed to hand over to the Mac each second flattened out at about 168,000, and everything above that was dropped.

Why did this not happen on my SSD? What was the only difference I could find? Bursts!

When the Mac reads data from a USB 3 device, the device sends some packets, then has to wait for the Mac to say “lgtm, send more!”. The SSD enclosure sends 16 packets before needing a go-ahead message back. The RTL8156B in my Ethernet adapter sends 4.

Here is a diagram of my best understanding of why this is an matter. I made this diagram 100 times, and I think I can probably improve it more, but if it helps you understand the issue, I have done my job.

Industry observers note that as you can see, the speed of packets coming into the adapter is 2.5 Gbps. That’s what the router pushes in. The speed going out is around 2 Gbps. The reason is that if you add up the average time it takes to get the go-ahead through my monitor’s hub, which is around 7.6 µs, to the average time it takes to send 4 KB, around 8.2 µs, you can find what the maximum speed is.

Well, if the speed of the drain from my adapter to my Mac is half a gig slower than the speed of the input, then you can imagine the buffer getting filled more and more until it overflows. Those are dropped packets, which result in a hard backoff when the router resends them, so you drop loads in speed. And that’s the reason for all of this.

I have a cupboard full of USB-C Ethernet adapters. Don’t ask.

Recent findings suggest that the problem is they’re all 1 gig adapters, so any of the tests I made would not tell me anything, because the issues don’t start at 1 gig. They start at around 2… If I run my 2.5 gig adapter at 1 gig speeds, I get 1 gig downloads with the official driver. If I run it at 1.5, I get 1.5. If I run it at 2, well, I get 1….

Recent findings suggest that so I thought I would do what any human would do, and I spent more money on a new adapter. Another UGREEN, but this time it’s one that promises 5 Gbps and uses the RTL8157 chip instead: UGREEN 5G USB-C Ethernet adapter. My reasoning was that if this one could get me better speeds, it would help me understand how. And that it did!

With this adapter, I dropped 0 frames:.

Why? Well, looking through what each adapter tells me about itself:.

I can see that instead of sending 4 1 KB packets per burst, it would send 8! And the speed of the link was also 2x faster, so those 8 KB would go 2x faster to the Mac. That means the time spent was 8 times lower to send the same data, and while the wait for the go-ahead was identical, the theoretical speed from the adapter to the Mac, including the wait for the go-ahead, was a maximum of 4.5 Gbps. That’s much bigger than the 2.5 coming into the adapter, so the buffer would never fill up, packets would never drop and everything was great, even if the “go-ahead” response was still much slower than when connected directly to the Mac.

In a recent development, I think the big takeaway from this is that all the things you think are quite easy to understand, such as transfer speeds, have so many cool intricacies that it’s worth diving deep every so often. Who would’ve thought that the speed of the link between the adapter and the Mac was defined not only by the link speed itself in Gbps, but also by the time it took your Mac to reply, by the amount of packets, by the speed of those packets, by the number of packets in a burst, and by the size of those packets?

See you next time, when I will spend just as much time on another trivial thing that we can all learn from!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A jury found a former Los Angeles resident guilty of starting what became the deadly Palisades Fire of January 2025, the city’s most destructive wildfire in its history.

According to recent reports, jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, was convicted of one count of destruction of property by means of fire and one count of arson affecting property used in interstate commerce. Federal prosecutors accused Rinderknecht of intentionally starting the original blaze, known as the Lachman fire. While the initial fire was quickly suppressed, unbeknownst to firefighters and other authorities at the time, embers of it continued to burn underground. On Jan. 7, heavy winds reignited the fire, causing it to surface and spread. The ensuing Palisades fire was one of the most destructive wildfires in Los Angeles history, killing 12 people and decimating 23,448 acres of land and nearly 7,000 structures across the Pacific Palisades region.

According to recent reports, “Twelve people lost their lives and thousands lost their homes because of Jonathan Rinderknecht’s malicious conduct,” remarked Attorney General Todd Blanche in a statement. “Thanks to the persistence and hard work of our prosecutors in the Central District of California, he will be held accountable.”.

In a recent development, “Jonathan Rinderknecht deliberately ignited a fire that killed 12 people and devastated an entire community,” stated First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli. “We were determined to hold him accountable, and today’s guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended.”.

After a federal jury in June deadlocked in favor of acquittal in Rinderknecht’s first trial in June, federal prosecutors narrowed their case to charge him with the two arson-related felonies rather than the three charges in the mistrial.

According to recent reports, steve Haney, the man’s lawyer for both trials, told the Los Angeles Times that they planned to appeal Friday’s verdict. “We are disappointed in the verdict, but respect the jury process,” Haney told the publication. “After a lengthy deliberation, they clearly gave this case a great deal of consideration.” Trending Stories Patrick Stewart Cause of Death Revealed Selena Gomez Shares Her Reaction to Martin Short Ruining Her Wedding Cake ‘Yes, Dear’ Star Anthony Clark's Cause of Death Revealed Marlon Jackson Reveals Stage 4 Prostate Cancer Diagnosis Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century.

Industry observers note that the prosecution argued that Rinderknecht, who was working on New Year’s Eve as an Uber driver on Dec. 31, 2024, was angry and frustrated because he was unable to find companionship on New Year’s. According to an affidavit from an investigator for the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, two of his passengers described him as “agitated and angry” that night. He allegedly drove to a Pacific Palisades trailhead, where he repeatedly listened to and watched a music video for the rap song, “Un Zder, Un Thé,” about despair, and tried calling an old friend, but was unable to connect with them.Prosecutors noted that Rinderknecht started the Lachman Fire just after midnight, and that around 12:12 a.m. on Jan. 1, 2025, environmental sensing platforms indicated the Lachman fire had begun. They said that Rinderknecht called 911 several times, but didn’t get through because his iPhone was out of range. By the time he finally connected with the police, the fire had already been reported by others in the neighborhood.

During his call with police, per the affidavit, Rinderknecht also allegedly typed a question into ChatGPT: “Are you at fault if a fire is lift [sic] because of your cigarette?” ChatGPT allegedly responded “Yes.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meta employees have expressed concerns about what appear to be major privacy breaches when using Muse, currently the second most popular free iPhone app in the App Store with over 10 million downloads.

This includes again accessing end-to-end encrypted messaging without permission, and sharing what may be the bank balances of another Muse user ….

Siri AI was not the only AI app to launch back in September; Meta’s Muse AI app was rolled out the same month, with the company describing it as “your personal AI agent that gets things done across every part of life.”.

Sources indicate that muse initially launched as an iPhone app, with Mac and iPad apps following shortly afterwards. It immediately moved to the top of the US App Store charts, overtaking ChatGPT. It promptly exceeded 5 million downloads following a major advertising push by Meta, and that number has since doubled.

Recent findings suggest that it wasn’t long before major privacy concerns were raised. Tech writer Jason Aten reported that the Mac app accessed his messages despite him explicitly refusing permission. The app then lied to him about how it had achieved this. Meta described this as a bug.

Security researcher Patrick Wardle also discovered a zero-day vulnerability that could allow an attacker to hijack dictated prompts, directing them instead to their own server.

I remarked at the time that I would absolutely not be one of the millions of people using the app, and the wisdom of that decision has now been underlined by a fresh report.

It has been revealed that reuters now reports Meta employees discussing further breaches. This includes another example of accessing encrypted messages without permission.

An employee using Muse on her personal phone reported it had surprised her with a reminder to respond to a message from her sister on Signal, an end-to-end encrypted messaging service popular with privacy advocates that competes with Meta’s WhatsApp.

“This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” the employee said in her post.

The report notes this appears to have been done by capturing push notifications. However, this was what the app claimed had happened in the earlier case, and it turned out not to be true. The AI Now Institute was able to replicate the problem of Muse accessing Signal messages without permission.

Another employee reported receiving unsolicited bank balances that they say appeared to be those of another Muse user.

Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I have never shared my bank account with Muse and never discussed any banking topic with Muse. I’m afraid it’s sending other’s bank info to me,” the staffer wrote in his post.

In a recent development, meta told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents” and suggested that the bank balances may have been AI hallucinations rather than leaked information. Enhancement: Meta has now told us that the balances were definitely hallucinations.

Recent findings suggest that "AI Agent" = Malware. There are an expanding number of "I told it not to do that" cases.

Sources indicate that the instructions (prompt) you give the agent are a tiny fraction of the total prompt context the agent uses, and Meta/Grok/etc. is not going to let you see that context. Agents harvesting your data (ex. see full disk access) and sending it to the mothership is just another revenue/training stream. Even if you are paying you are still the product.

Meta has taken concern with the messaging claims. It indicates that access to either notifications or messaging must be explicitly granted.

With Android, users have the option to grant apps notification access, which allows apps to see notifications as they’re received. This is something users need to opt in to and is not specific to Muse. With Mac, to allow Muse to work on your behalf, you not only need to click allow for accessibility and screen recording, but after that it takes you to a settings screen where you once again need to confirm and turn this on.

The firm also implies that the experience of employees may relate to internal versions of Muse.

Employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.

I can only repeat my previous take on Muse: Nope.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • T here’s not a room in the world that could fit all of the trinkets, gifts, and prized possessions comedian Leslie Jones has accumulated through her career.
  • Sources indicate that “I always keep something,” Jones claims on Zoom from her Los Angeles home, panning the camera to show a wall of white shelves packed to the brim with tchotchkes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

T here’s not a room in the world that could fit all of the trinkets, gifts, and prized possessions comedian Leslie Jones has accumulated through her career.

Sources indicate that “I always keep something,” Jones claims on Zoom from her Los Angeles home, panning the camera to show a wall of white shelves packed to the brim with tchotchkes. But it’s hard for her to pick favorites — especially since they all have treasured memories that go along with them. “Colin [Jost] gave me a trophy that mentioned ‘Baddest Bitch in the World,’” she says with a laugh, pointing at the memento. “I’ve still got that one.”.

Jones might be one of the best-known late-bloomers in show business. In 2014, she joined Saturday Night Live as a writer before being promoted to a featured player. She was 47 at the time, making her the oldest person ever to join the cast. But even with two decades of stand-up work under her belt, slogging through bombed sets, late-night performances, and side hustles, Jones notes she doesn’t regret her winding path to comedy fame. In fact, she’s adamant that if success had happened for her any sooner, she wouldn’t be here to talking to us. “I would have been a cautionary tale,” she says, plainly. “I would have made all the wrong decisions.”.

Sources indicate that jones spent five seasons on SNL, where she established herself as a comedic voice known for taking wild — and often foul-mouthed — swings at everything from dating during slavery to abortion bans to prepares for her own funeral. This brash self-assuredness followed her even after her tenure, as she expanded her résumé to include TV and film roles in projects like Ghostbusters and Coming 2 America as well as professional fan duties — Chief Super Fan Commentator, to be precise — for NBC’s Olympics broadcasts. From her Upcoming York Times-bestselling memoir Leslie Fcking Jones to her latest gig hosting HGTV’s Roast My Rental (which debuted over the summer and re-airs through the end of November, and can be streamed on HBO Max), Jones has cemented herself as an outspoken and hilarious presence in pretty much any medium. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century.

“I’m making it work,” she notes. “There’s no such thing as not waking up and getting some shit done.”.

For Rolling Stone’s Last Word column, Jones talked through nearly blowing off her SNL audition, vacation horror stories, and how to end the political divide in America.

What was your first job as a teenager?Damn, that took me way back. I worked at this place called Lounge Car Tours. My mom worked in accounting or something and she got me a job cleaning the buses. She tried to teach me how to drive her car, which was a stick, and I ran into one of the buses.

Recent findings suggest that when did you realize comedy was for you? The first time I touched the mic. In college [at Colorado State University], I did the “funniest person on campus” contest. Whoever won got to open up for the comedians that were coming into town. When I was at that contest, I [felt] like, “Oh, I’ve already been doing this 10 years.”.

What’s the worst experience you’ve had bombing at a show?It was six months into me performing. This dude in the audience started heckling. I bombed and then I went back the next week. He was there, he didn’t say a word, and I still bombed.

In a recent development, how do you handle hecklers now? I tear they ass up. It depends on what type of heckler it is. If it’s a nice heckler, I’ll do something fun. But if it’s a mean or rude heckler, I try to make them feel like they’ll never speak again in public.

According to recent reports, what’s something you wish you had known early in your career?I don’t think I would have wanted to know, because I like that I learned my way. Maybe not to just make friends so easily. Don’t trust so easily. Related Content ‘SNL’: Watch Phoebe Bridgers Perform ‘Bobby,’ ‘Still Standing’ ‘SNL’: Hippie John Mulaney Has Some Very Unhip Thoughts at Woodstock ‘SNL’ Weekend Patch Roasts Trump Admin Over Grounded Flights, Jensen Huang Affairs ‘SNL’ Cold Open: Jensen Huang, Tech CEOs Get a Crash Course in Female Spies.

According to recent reports, what was the first big purchase that you made with your comedy money?Don’t laugh. I bought this Michael Kors purse. It was $300. I thought I was the shit. Then my friend was like, “Bitch, that’s just a Michael Kors purse. That’s not no Louis [Vuitton]. The fuck is wrong with you?”.

How does it feel in your body when you get a laugh from an audience?Like a high. Adrenaline. It’s a great feeling — ticklish.

What’s the best advice you’ve ever gotten? November of ’87, I performed at this place called the World Comedy Club [in Times Square]. This comedian named Speedy had a show. Speedy’s best friends with Jamie Foxx, so Jamie came to close the show for him. I did that show. Did terrible. Bombed. I remember watching Jamie perform, going, “I got to figure out how he does this.” I had him in the corner like, “How do I become a better comic?” He was like, “How old are you?” I was 19. He was like, “You’re a baby. You don’t know anything. You don’t have no jokes. Go and live your life. Get your heart broken. Break hearts. Get fired. Get hired. Go live a life so you can have something to talk about.”.

In a recent development, did you take the advice? Yeah. I was working. I was never trying to get a job to try to find myself — I was always trying to get a job to make money. I think young people have that equation wrong. I worked at Denny’s and then I sold perfume in the parking lot. I worked at the justice of the peace for a little, then the post office. Then I waitressed at Spoons [Grill & Bar, in Orange County]. I think I waited on [SNL cast member] Mikey Day while I was there. He used to go there all the time! I feel like I waited on him because [once I got to SNL], he had an obsession with me with his sketches. He would write sketches every time where I was either yelling at him or beating him up. I was like, “Mikey, do you want me to beat you up? Is this a thing you have?”.

Recent findings suggest that what’s your strongest memory from your SNL audition? Chris Rock got me the audition. He came in [to the Comedy Store in L.A.] one night, saw me perform, and then called me like two days later and was like, “Hey, I just had dinner with Lorne Michaels and he’s gonna call you for an audition for SNL.” I know he expected me to go crazy, but my brother had just died and I didn’t care about shit. When he called me, I went off on him. He said, “You’re a dumbass. Go to the fucking audition and do some jokes” and hung up. I called my manager livid — ”Fucking Chris Rock got me a fucking audition for SNL. How dare he?” My manager was like, “OK, I’m gonna need you to take a second to shut the fuck up. Have you lost your mind? Leslie, if you don’t go to that audition, I will quit.” I go to the Comedy Store just knowing I’m gonna find somebody that’s going to agree with me. And every comedian up there was looking at me like [I was] the dumbest motherfucker.

Industry observers note that we know how it ended — you were on the show for five seasons — but how did you spin that attitude in the room with Lorne?I was like, “You know what? I’m a go, so I can show them that I don’t need this shit.” Oh, God, the arrogance! By the end of that week, I wanted that job. I was so wrong. “There’s so much shit I can learn here.”.

I remember being in Indianapolis on the phone with my manager, and my manager was like, “Yeah, I think they’re gonna go with someone else, homie.” And I was like, “Yeah, I think so, too.” I was depressed. I was like, “Fuck. Do I take this job that my aunt is offering me? Because if I keep doing this, I ain’t gonna have no retirement money. I ain’t gonna be able to take care of myself when I get older. I’m 47 already, so maybe I should just go on back to Memphis and she can get me a job.” Then they called me.

In a recent development, how did you decide it was time to leave SNL?People try to act like they don’t know when they’re supposed to leave a situation. You know when you’re supposed to leave your job. You know when it’s time to move to the next level. If I was there when I was in my twenties, I would have stayed a long, long time just because I needed to learn and make money and get the connections. But [Lorne] got me when I was 47. And after five years of being there, I wasn’t ready to settle for that being my job the rest of my life. So it was, “If I don’t leave right now, I won’t be able to leave.”.

Sources indicate that during the 2024 Paris Olympics, you were NBC’s Chief Super Fan Commentator. Are there any Olympic sports you feel you could make a solid attempt at?Oh, hell, no! Nah. The Olympics is the best of the best. There’s nothing I could do — maybe [jumping] around with the little ribbon.

Sources indicate that on HGTV’s Roast My Rental, you help people fix up short-term homes. Do you have any of your own vacation-home or rental horror stories?Oh, yeah! I stayed in a place where they had a beehive in the wall. Then he had the nerve to say “Those bees wasn’t there before you got there.” Oh, so I brought the hive and climbed down a mountain, scaled up on the wall, and stuck that beehive right behind the bed? Yeah, that’s what I did.

Recent findings suggest that who are some people who’ve encouraged or supported you through your career? When I met them, they gave me great advice: Whoopi Goldberg, Arsenio Hall, Damon Wayans. Bill Bellamy, Greg Fitzsimmons. So many comedians.

How do you approach romantic relationships?What is that? A candy bar? That’s why I’m single now. I don’t approach them. I burn them down. I don’t know. You tell me.

Is there an album that corresponds to meaningful or transformative times in your life?Stevie Wonder, Talking Book. It has “Visions,” one of the best songs ever written. It’s the most beautiful, beautiful song. Stevie Wonder and Donny Hathaway are very vital to me. I love music. My dad loved music. For a long time, he thought I was gonna be a musician because I knew music so well, just like he knew it. That’s back in the day when people used to write songs, write poetry. Now it’s just about how fast they can get into somebody’s drawers.

According to recent reports, are there any projects you’ve turned down that you wish you’d said yes to?No. There’s projects that I said yes to that I wish I said no to.

What are some of those?I ain’t gonna mention them. My publicist will be like, “God dammit, Leslie!”.

What’s a performance you’re proudest of? All my [Weekend] Updates on SNL. And there’s a sketch I did about the Upper East Side. I really am glad I did that — that’s one of my things I love the most.

According to recent reports, what are some rules that you live by?Don’t shit where I eat — meaning don’t fuck people you work with. It’s the Number One rule because you will fuck your shit up. Don’t lend money. Just give it, because waiting on people to pay you back, you’re just gonna be frustrated. Passion at all times. Do everything with passion. Even if you’re folding your clothes. I can tell a person’s character just by how they fold their clothes. Always be intentional and enjoy everything — don’t skip days. Don’t say, “Hey, I can’t wait until it’s Tuesday.” Enjoy the days up until Tuesday.

Industry observers note that do you think you could have handled fame if it had happened to you when you started comedy at 19? No, absolutely not. Oh, thank you, Jesus. Thank you, Lord, for not letting me make it at 19. When you get stuff young, you stop creating. You stop growing. It’s good for a child to grow up. No one should get things before it’s time. I’ve seen so many comedians crash because they get that stuff early. I’m glad that I went through the stuff that I went through, because when I did get famous, I knew how to handle it. I don’t think I would have been that way at 19. Oh, God, the scandals! I would have fucked everybody. I’m serious. What’s your advice to people who want to get into comedy or entertainment? Don’t look at the now. Look at the how. I didn’t just pop up. There’s no such thing as an overnight success, and there’s no such thing as sacrificing everything so you can make it. If you’re trying to make it, still get a job, pay your fucking rent, pay your fucking taxes, get some goddamn health insurance, live a regular life. Don’t be a starving artist — there’s no fucking such thing. And whatever craft that you’re going into, you are not better than that craft. That craft has been there way before you, and it will be there way after you’re dead. So, don’t think that you’re better than the craft of comedy. Bow to the craft.

It has been revealed that you’re no stranger to mixing comedy and politics. What are your thoughts on America’s current political moment? I want everybody to understand that the reason that we have so much hate right now is because we don’t have love for ourselves individually. You can’t give something that you don’t have. I know that sounds like a cliché, but you have to start loving yourself. Every part — your insecurities, your badness, your mistakes, your flaws, your wonderfulness, all of that. The only way we’re gonna beat all of this hate is if everyone starts having a full, solid love for themselves. Because when you love yourself and actually like yourself, you don’t want to hurt nobody. And then you will get your ass up and go vote.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In light of growing pushback from users who want more control over how AI is integrated into their apps (if at all), Canva is introducing new settings that let them hide generative AI features and see less AI-generated content. Here are the details.

Canva today revealed fresh controls that will let Free and Pro users choose whether to see generative AI features across the app, as well as how much AI-generated content appears in search results and in recommendations for templates and design elements.

The company notes that both controls are available at no additional cost and can be turned on or off at any time.

According to Canva, “the future of creativity isn’t a choice between AI and no AI.” For this reason, it is introducing the following controls:.

The firm says that, while it knows that there is an ongoing debate between consumers with opposing views on whether AI has a place in creative work, it thinks “both views are valid”:.

“It’s not our place to tell anyone how to create, so today we’re launching two new controls that put that decision firmly with our community […].”.

Importantly, the company noted that select features that use AI without generating fresh content will remain available even when generative AI features are turned off:.

Sources indicate that “Some of Canva’s everyday editing tools use AI to make simple tasks faster, without generating anything upcoming. Background Remover, one of Canva’s most popular tools, lifts a subject cleanly out of a photo in a single click, and Magic Grab lets creators select an object in an image and move it somewhere else in the design. Both remain available when the generative AI switch is off, because they work only with what’s already in a design.”.

Canva added that these tools also won’t add an AI label to a design’s metadata, since that label is reserved for AI-generated content.

As for the organization’s design content library, Canva noted that while “a small portion of the library is AI-generated content made by Canva, including some abstract backgrounds and illustrated graphics,” its community has told it “they want an easier way to find design assets made by real people, so the content control reduces the number of AI-generated templates and elements that appear in search results and recommendations.”.

With today’s announcement, Canva is essentially expanding on the AI permissions already available to administrators of Business, Enterprise, Teams, and Education accounts, which let organizations control how their teams use AI.

Industry News: Six Things You Should Do Now to Optimize Your Setup for GTA 6

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1162 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that you’re almost ready for Grand Theft Auto VI.
  • Industry observers note that GTA 6 is absurdly large.
  • It has been revealed that alternatively, it’s pretty easy to add more storage (if you can afford it).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that you’re almost ready for Grand Theft Auto VI. You’ve preloaded the game on your console, you’ve taken the next month off work, and you’ve locked your phone in a Faraday cage and set it adrift at sea. You’re prepared to lock in, and you haven’t forgotten a thing…right? Well, just to make sure, here are the most important tips to optimize your setup before you fire up the most anticipated game of the decade.

Industry observers note that GTA 6 is absurdly large. According to Rockstar, you’ll need up to 212GB of storage space. For high-end consoles like the PS5 Pro, that’s more than 10% of the available storage space, and close to half the space on the more budget-conscious Xbox Series S. There’s a good chance you’ll have to delete something to make room.

It has been revealed that alternatively, it’s pretty easy to add more storage (if you can afford it). External SSDs are probably the cheapest route, though you’ll want to make sure to use a high-speed USB cable to connect it. It’s even worth shopping around for alternate models of SSD. For example, at the time of writing, the popular 2TB WD_BLACK external drive was close to $200, but the exact same drive in pink was $132.

Recent findings suggest that you can also directly upgrade the storage of your console with expansion drives. The Xbox Series X|S supports proprietary expansion cards, while the PS5 and PS5 Pro can accept most M.2 internal SSDs. These will generally be faster, since they plug directly into the console via higher-speed connections than a drive hooked up via USB.

Let’s face it: Half the fun of any sandbox game is the weird, unique stuff that happens to only you. So you’re probably going to be hitting that “record recent gameplay” button more often than usual. While you’re cleaning up your storage space (or adding more), make sure to account for all the video clips you might want to save.

According to recent reports, file size of video clips depends on a lot of factors, but 4K recordings can generally take up to 0.5GB per minute of footage. You can cut that down by saving footage in 1080p instead, but either way you’ll want to leave a little extra space.

Sources indicate that game footage is also a pretty good place to look if you need to make room on your console and don’t want to delete any games. Be honest with yourself: You don’t need all those clips from Horizon Forbidden West you saved four years ago. Dive into the settings on your console and find the biggest media files you forgot you even had on there.

It has been revealed that according to Rockstar, GTA 6 will be targeting 30fps across consoles at launch, which is pretty low as modern AAA games go. Part of the reason for that is all the processing power going to rendering a complex environment, but it also means you won’t need a fancy high frame rate TV or monitor any time soon to get the most out of it. Still, it couldn’t hurt to check a few settings on your display.

Sources indicate that first, make sure you’re using a higher refresh rate than 30Hz. While the game is targeting 30fps, it is technically capable of more, so if your console can keep up, you don’t want to accidentally bottleneck your frames. This setting will vary by device, so check the manual that came with your screen.

Sources indicate that also, make sure you have HDR enabled on your hardware. There’s a good chance this is already turned on for your TV, but sometimes other devices can switch display modes if they only support SDR. The game will help you calibrate your HDR settings for GTA 6 specifically when you launch it, but only if it detects HDR compatibility in the first place.

If you’re planning to buy a console specifically for GTA 6, this might be one of those rare instances where a PS5 Pro really is worth the upgrade. According to Rockstar, certain features like ray-traced shadows will only be available on the Pro version of Sony’s console.

More importantly, the PS5 Pro version supports PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (or PSSR), which upscales lower-resolution images to get better detail and higher frame rates out of the same hardware. Given that GTA 6 is already starting at a meager target of 30fps on most consoles, anything that can give your frame rate a boost is probably going to feel like a welcome improvement over the baseline.

In a recent development, I’ll tell you a secret as someone who’s spent a lot of time testing different game controllers: Most of the time, you really don’t need an expensive “elite” controller. Most of the time. I don’t buy into the idea that a taller control stick is going to make you an esports athlete. It can be nice to have, but it’s not a game changer. What does matter is customizing your controls, especially for long gaming sessions.

The DualSense Edge wireless controller is a favorite of mine, mainly because of the rear paddles and adjustable triggers. The former lets you map any button to a rear lever that you can access with your fingers underneath the controller, which can often ease some of the wrist strain of awkward button combos. And the adjustable triggers let you activate the buttons with less motion, again reducing repetitive stress.

Sources indicate that the Xbox Elite Series 2 controller has similar features for the Xbox, as well as custom caps for the D-pad. Both consoles’ versions of pro controllers are more expensive than the standard ones, but if you’re planning to game for many hours, it can be worth it to get a controller that’s more comfortable for you.

Recent findings suggest that if you have an Xbox One, you don’t necessarily have to upgrade your console to play GTA 6, but you might want to take a look at your network. GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on day one, and you’ll be able to stream the game to an Xbox One console (as long as you purchase Cloud playtime as well or get some with your Game Pass subscription). This is the only way to play on a console older than the current generation, so if you don’t want to shell out for latest hardware, this might be your best bet.

It has been revealed that xbox recommends a minimum of a 20Mbps connection to run cloud gaming, but more is obviously better. If you can connect your console to a wired Ethernet connection, that would be better and provide more stability. If you can’t connect a cable, then at least make sure you’re well within range of your wifi router, and try to limit any other bandwidth-hogging applications on the network while you’re playing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“I write behind the wheel of the van,” Jason Scott, leader of the namesake band Jason Scott and the High Heat, says. “There’s no other time.”.

Sources indicate that bassist Ryan Magnani, however, calls bullshit: The van is just one of the places that Scott, a prolific Oklahoma writer, is able to come up with material. “Just the other day, you came off of a drive and you said, ‘I think I just wrote a cool song.’ And I am looking around like, ‘Where did you write a song? You don’t have a guitar,’” Magnani states. ‘You said, ‘Nah, I was just thinking about it.’”.

Sources indicate that jason Scott and the High Heat released their latest album Play Boy back in September, marking their second record on the Leo33 label and their second in just over a year, following the March 2025 drop of American Grin. Scott has spent the better part of a decade writing songs shaped by his Pentecostal upbringing and the personal and artistic awakenings he had after pursuing music full-time, but Play Boy goes hard in a different direction. It’s best described as “Jason Scott, unfiltered,” a collection of songs written on whims.

“It has no inherent meaning, and it did not come from anywhere,” Scott says, “other than, ‘That’s all we be doin’ out here.’”.

With Scott on guitar and vocals and Magnani on bass, the High Heat features Gabriel Mor on guitar, Garrison Brown on guitar and keys, and Tremaine “Bobby” Wade on drums. Taylor Johnson, a one-time member, is the band’s producer. On this particular afternoon, they are gathered around a table at an Irish pub on Manhattan’s Upper West Side, coming in hot from a European run and gearing up for a CBS Saturday Morning taping the next day. Together, the High Heat are a group of misfits from Oklahoma capable of being sincere in one moment, and irreverent in the next.

According to recent reports, the group skewed toward the latter when they introduced Play Boy to the world in early summer by releasing the twangy “Shit Show” and its accompanying video.
